text: Seventy-three minutes, most of them on the water, and every one of them borrowed. Natan is five; his mother is taking him to Rome; his father Jorge has the weeks before the move and spends them out at the Chinchorro reef, fishing, sailing, handing the boy a mask. Documentary, family and drama are all listed for it at once, which is less a hedge than a description of the method: nothing staged as event, everything arranged. The Mayan inheritance the film is after does not arrive as explanation. It arrives as work — bait cut, lines hauled, a surface read from above and from underneath. What is at stake is not whether father and son get along. It is how much of a place and a way of living in it a man can hand over before a scheduled departure, and how much of that a five-year-old can carry to another continent.

Six stories share one film, and none of them is closed off by the story that follows; what passes between them is a motif rather than a plot. Petr Zelenka works in black humour with a bitter edge — an ancient curse, infidelity, private deviations, an unexpected miracle, forgiveness handed out by people in no position to hand it out. Each part has its own atmosphere and its own method, so the register keeps shifting on purpose, and an object or a gesture from one story turns up two stories later seen from the other side. The Czech Lions it collected for film, direction and screenplay indicate where the weight sits: in the construction, in what is planted in one place and collected in another. A hundred and two minutes, filed as comedy, and the comedy is not there to soften anything.

A high school after hours, a student practising alone, and then the building keeps her voice and nothing else. The premise is set out that plainly: a girl who wants to sing is killed, her body is not found, and what remains of her is held inside the school where no one can see it. One friend can hear her. A school is efficient equipment for horror — corridors that empty on a schedule, rooms built for practising alone, a place designed so that a girl can be by herself in it without anyone thinking she is unattended. The real problem the film sets itself is one of point of view. A ghost who can only be heard cannot haunt in the usual manner; she has to speak, and be believed, and the friend at the other end of that voice has to decide what to do with information she cannot show to anybody.

A film can cover twenty-four hours and still decline to make anything happen; this one does it in Montevideo, with three young men in the street. Character over narrative is the stated preference, and that costs something, because scenes which advance nothing have to hold on their own terms. What fills them is waiting: errands that lead nowhere, a conversation resumed hours after it was dropped, an afternoon spent working out what an afternoon is for. Ninety-four minutes lets the boredom register without letting it become the subject, and the comedy does protective work over material that is not funny underneath. Three people have arrived at the age when the question of what a life is supposed to consist of turns up for the first time, and nobody within walking distance has an answer worth having.

Sebastian wants to be a woman, Andreas is certain that he is not gay, and the film sets itself down in the gap between those two statements. Neither one cancels what is between them; that is the difficulty the eighty-four minutes exist for. Stockholm supplies grit rather than glamour, a city where two people can pass unremarked in public and have nothing settled in private. Sebastian's self-abuse is there in the premise, which keeps the stakes physical — what is being risked is not a relationship but a body, and the terms on which it can be lived in. Romance as a genre tends to promise that feeling will resolve. Here the feeling is not the problem. The problem is that the two of them have no shared vocabulary for what they are to each other, and no one is offering to supply one.

A Japanese feature from 1996 spends two hours and nine minutes on a schoolboy's unspoken crush, and treats the length as necessary rather than generous. Shuji wants Hiroyuki. Hiroyuki has noticed Kasane, who has just transferred into the class. The geometry is ordinary; the patience is not. At that runtime a whole term can pass on screen, friendships can shift by degrees, the same three can sit in the same room for weeks with nothing said, so that anything finally said comes with all of it behind. The stakes are proportionate to adolescence, which is to say total: not whether the feeling is returned, but whether Shuji can go on standing in that classroom afterwards. It carries a Tiger Award, a mark on the record beside a story that never raises its voice.

The transaction at the centre is stated without euphemism: a man takes money from other men for the sight of his granddaughter's body. Beside it runs a second strand, someone who falls in love with the girl, and that is where the difficulty starts, since tenderness is not an exit from the arrangement — it grows in the same ground, among the same people. Eighty minutes is brief for a drama built on this, and the brevity reads as refusal: it holds the film to a length at which nobody can be redeemed and nothing has time to soften. Cláudio Assis treats the situation as a standing condition rather than an incident, something already in place when the film starts and not waiting on anybody's decision. Nothing in it is decorative. The discomfort is not a side effect; it is the argument.

A man loses his job, and the film takes up the plain question of what the remaining hours are for. The premise is barely a premise, and across ninety minutes it is inhabited rather than extended, which is the point: the drama sits in the interval between one kind of work and the next, when a person is willing to be useful and is required by nobody. The title names a crane, a machine for lifting what a body cannot, run by someone who is himself easy to replace. Argentina in 2000 is where this happens, and the film keeps to that scale — one man, his days, the arrangements he makes and remakes. What stands to be lost is not income. It is standing: how a man is spoken to, and how he answers, once what he does has moved into the past tense.

The tyrant is dead before the film has a plot, and his farmhands own the land in equal shares, which turns out to be the harder arrangement. An Austrian farming valley at the start of the twentieth century, small enough that every hour of anyone's labour is visible to everyone else: the servants are relieved, then they are landowners, then they find that a household without a master still needs somebody to say when the harvest comes in. Nobody has to obey. Nobody can compel. Austria put it forward as its international submission to the Academy Awards, one country's choice of what to send abroad about land and who is owed it. Ninety-five minutes, and the pressure comes less from inside the farm than from the valley around it, which has its own opinion about who should be holding land.

In Bosnia a debt is not collected at a funeral, and the film opens with a man who does it anyway. Fikret is sixteen. At the burial service for his father a stranger named Hamid states what the dead man owed and refuses to let the sum go into the ground, so by the ordinary working of the custom the debt is now the son's and the humiliation is the whole family's. Sarajevo in the years after the war is where he goes to find money — a city short of most things and not short of people prepared to make him an offer. Srđan Vuletić keeps the boy's own terms almost religious: he speaks of redeeming his father's soul and means it, though the only thing he can actually redeem is a figure. A hundred and five minutes of a child moving through adult arrangements, each worse than it first looks.

The errand is a reunion, and the man conducting it is the reason there is anyone to go and find. A father who drinks and is violent sets out to bring back the boy's mother, who left him, and the boy goes along — not as company, more as a witness who can neither be left behind nor be of any use. Seventy-four minutes in Tamil, and the journey is the entire event: a distance crossed, a temper carried across it, a child working out in silence how far it is back. India entered it as an international submission to the Academy Awards and it holds a Tiger Award. What is at risk is not whether the mother is found. It is what the boy is learning, mile by mile, to expect from grown men, and how much of that he will still be carrying when the walking stops.

The parents do not announce it; their daughter assembles it from the way they speak in front of her over four days away. A Chilean family sets off on a short holiday, and the girl, still young enough to be told nothing directly, works out that the marriage may be ending. The information reaches her by inference, and Dominga Sotomayor builds the film to match — the vantage stays low and partial, at the level where half of every adult sentence goes over a head. Ninety-six minutes on a trip that has already been decided somewhere else. Nothing needs to happen for the stakes to be complete: the family is intact for the length of the journey, and the girl has begun to suspect this is the last of its kind, which turns every ordinary hour of the holiday into something she is holding on to.

The premise is one sentence long — two ghosts walk the Camino of Santiago — and the film shows no interest in lengthening it. Eighty minutes, spoken in Catalan, given over to a pilgrimage made by figures with no body to tire and no death in front of them, which removes nearly everything that ordinarily gives such a walk its meaning. What is left is road, weather, distance, and the obligation to keep going because the route keeps going. It is filed as drama, and the label sits oddly, since there is not much conflict available to travellers who cannot be harmed. The pressure falls instead on talk and on terrain: what the dead still find worth discussing, and how strange an ordinary Spanish hillside looks when the things crossing it are not alive.

The village comes first and the people second, which is what a portrait means: the shape of the thing is a place, not a story. Moravia, a small settlement, inhabitants described as quirky — a word that usually carries condescension and does not have to. A hundred and fourteen minutes gives each of them time to become more than a single trait, and lets the comedy sit alongside the drama without either one taking charge. Little is scheduled to occur, so the weight falls on observation: proximity, habit, who ends up in the same room as whom, year after year, and what that does to people who cannot easily get away from each other. The Czech Republic sent it out as its international submission to the Academy Awards, a country presenting itself through a village it does not flatter.
